transcript:
HEADER:
Date: 2027-03-22
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Khan (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (CTO, SolarPay), Emily Chen (Lead ML Eng, SolarPay), Marcus Gomez (Platform Ops, SolarPay)

SUMMARY (auto-generated, may be rough):
Redwood ran an Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and KV/prefix caching with a cost model tailored to SolarPay's payments workloads. Customer called out tight p95 latency targets (150-200ms), high QPS for payments routing, and strict data residency + KMS requirements. Discussed hosted vs dedicated, VPC private deployment, and tradeoffs between aggressive KV cache sizes and memory footprint. Agreed next steps: share cost model spreadsheet, provision trial dedicated node, Emily to send prompt/seq distribution.

TOPICS: batching, KV cache, prefix caching, cost model, dedicated vs hosted, SOC2/KMS, trial benchmark

TRANSCRIPT:
[00:00] Aisha: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm aisha from redwood, i'm the ae on this account, we got marcus from se with me, marcus do you want to intro?
[00:06] Marcus (SE): sure hi all marcus here, i'll run through the optimize walkthrough - batching and kv cache - and we'll show a simple cost model for solarpay's traffic patterns.
[00:15] Ravi: great, thanks. quick note - we only have ~60 minutes, we've got a couple execs in back-to-back so if we need to cut we will. our main goals: keep p95 under 200ms for auth routing, and reduce per-token cost cause this will scale fast.
[00:28] Emily: also want to validate we can meet our encryption + KMS requirements, and if we need private deployment / vpc we need that in the plan.
[00:36] Marcus (SE): yep, all of that's on the table. quick qual questions - what's your current stack for models? are you running open models in house or hitting managed endpoints?
[00:45] Marcus Gomez: we run an in-house model infra for some features, but for routing we were considering a hosted api to move faster. latency is the large constraint, and we have a lot of short sequences (~32-128 tokens) for routing prompts.
[00:58] Marcus (SE): perfect - short seqs favor batching gains but small seqs also mean kv/prefix caching can be very effective for reuse. do you have any cache hits today?
[01:10] Ravi: we do a small LRU cache at the app level but nothing using kv cache at the model layer; user prompts for routing are highly repetitive - same merchant names, same intents - so hit rates should be good.
[01:22] Marcus (SE): okay that's promising. i'll show two levers: continuous batching (we'll call it dynamic batching) and prefix / kv cache. batching reduces gpu utilization per request by grouping concurrent requests; kv cache avoids recomputing prefix key/value states for repeated prefixes which is huge for short, repeated prompts.
[01:41] Emily: will kv cache increase memory requirements a lot? our infra is memory tight.
[01:46] Marcus (SE): yes tradeoff - kv cache is memory vs compute. we generally model it: a 1.2x memory bump for a moderate cache size gives up to 40-60% token cost reduction in our examples depending on hit rate. i'll pull the slide.
[02:01] [02:01] Marcus (SE): (screen share) slide 3 - here's the cost model input: qps, avg seq length, p95 latency target, cache hit rate assumptions, and batching window.
[02:15] Marcus (SE): for solarpay i plugged in 800 qps steady ramp to 2k at peak, avg seq 64 tokens, p95 target 200ms, and two configs: hosted optimized model vs dedicated with 8xA100 equiv.
[02:29] Ravi: can you clarify the batching window - we can't add more than 20ms of queuing or we fail slas.
[02:35] Marcus (SE): yes, we model batching windows in tens of ms. for your p95 target i'd recommend an aggressive batch limit of 10ms at the frontend plus dynamic flushing on latency tail. that typically gives you a 2-3x improvement in throughput while keeping p95 within your 200ms.
[02:50] Emily: 10ms sounds tight, do you have customers doing that?
[02:54] Marcus (SE): yes, with dedicated capacity and predictable load we see consistent 8-12ms median queueing. hosted can also hit that but dedicated is more predictable.
[03:05] [03:05] Marcus (SE): next point - prefix kv cache. if you have repeated prefixes and a 70% hit rate, effective tokens per request drop dramatically - we ran a back-of-envelope: 64 tokens avg -> effective 20 tokens on cache hit, so cost per request drops ~2.5-3x.
[03:25] Ravi: wow that would be huge. how do you handle cache eviction and cold start behavior?
[03:31] Marcus (SE): we support LRU + TTL eviction policies and also warm-start policies for known important prefixes. cold starts are mitigated by fallback to compute path; you can configure a hybrid where the first N minutes we warm the cache via background replay of common prefixes.
[03:46] Marcus Gomez: is that replay pulling PII into redwood systems? we need to ensure nothing sensitive is stored.
[03:53] Marcus (SE): good call - for private deployments or dedicated, cache entries can be encrypted at rest and keys managed by customer KMS; we also support tokenization/redaction at ingestion so you can avoid storing raw PII keys in the cache.
[04:06] Emily: do you have SOC2 docs for that flow?
[04:09] Aisha: yep, we'll share SOC2 + KMS architecture after - link in follow-up.
[04:15] [04:15] Marcus (SE): back to cost model - here's a table (slide) comparing hosted vs dedicated at your load with and without kv cache and with batching set to 10ms.
[04:26] Marcus (SE): hosted, no cache: est $0.045 per request; hosted with cache: $0.018 per request. dedicated no cache: $0.012 per request (amortized over reserved capacity), dedicated with cache: $0.005 per request. numbers are illustrative; we'll send a spreadsheet you can plug your real inputs into.
[04:47] Ravi: that delta to $0.005 is compelling. what's the commitment for dedicated?
[04:52] Aisha: dedicated is typically reserved capacity monthly contracts; we can do a short pilot for 2-4 weeks to benchmark with a small commitment, then scale. Marcus will provision a trial node.
[05:03] Emily: about model variants - do you support quantized model variants for lower mem?
[05:07] Marcus (SE): yes, we support int8 / q4 variants and model selection policies. smaller quantized variants reduce memory but may affect quality; Optimize can recommend quantization profile based on your prompt/eval set and show the perf/quality tradeoff.
[05:20] [05:20] Marcus (SE): now i want to show a simple simulation - i modeled hit rates 40%, 60%, 80% and mem footprint tradeoffs. (screen) at 60% hit rate we hit ~2.8x cost reduction with a 1.15x memory increase relative to base. at 80% hit we get close to 4x.
[05:40] Marcus Gomez: how do we measure hit rates in prod to validate these assumptions?
[05:45] Marcus (SE): you can enable metrics from our runtime - cache hit/miss counters, per-prefix stats, token-level cost breakdown. the console shows heatmaps and exportable CSVs. we'll give you access to a sandbox console for the trial.
[05:58] Ravi: and data residency - if we need EU-only - can that be enforced?
[06:03] Aisha: yes, dedicated can be region pinned or private (VPC) deployment; we also support on-prem for strict residency. we'll send the architecture options.
[06:12] Emily: one more thing: our prompts include merchant names which are PII-ish. if we do caching, can we ensure that those cache keys are hashed/obfuscated?
[06:21] Marcus (SE): absolutely, you can transform prefixes with a hashing/redaction step before they hit the cache; we also support deterministic tokenization so you still get hit aggregation for normalized prefixes.
[06:33] [06:33] Marcus (SE): quick live demo - i'll run a small benchmark script showing qps/latency with and without caching. give me a sec to flip contexts.
[06:41] [07:02] Marcus (SE): ok running the script now, baseline (no cache) at 800 qps - p95 ~185ms, tokens/req ~64, cpu/gpu util high. enabling kv cache with simulated 65% hit rate - p95 drops slightly to 170ms but cost drops substantially; with batching window 10ms effective throughput increases and p95 still within target.
[07:25] Emily: the p95 improving a bit surprises me - i expected cache to add tail risk.
[07:30] Marcus (SE): it can, if cache retrieval path adds overhead, but our implementation returns quickly for hits and avoids compute queuing which often reduces tail under high concurrency. that's why we prefer warm cache and small batching windows.
[07:44] Ravi: what's your recommended rollout path - do we flip caching on for everything at once?
[07:50] Marcus (SE): recommended: staged rollout - start with important prefixes only (e.g., routing-intent prefixes), monitor hit rates and tail latency, then expand. we also support canary percent rollouts and automatic fallback to compute path on tail degradation.
[08:04] Marcus Gomez: about monitoring - can we export the raw metrics to our prometheus?
[08:09] Marcus (SE): yes, we provide prometheus metrics endpoints and trace hooks; console additionally provides UI dashboards.
[08:16] Emily: any gotchas on cache invalidation if we change model versions?
[08:20] Marcus (SE): cache keys are model-version aware by default; when you roll a model it can either rebuild or reuse cache entries depending on compatibility. Optimize will flag incompatible kv formats.
[08:33] [08:33] Aisha: quick pause - i want to cover pricing/practicals. we typically need sample prompt set and avg seq length to produce the tailored spreadsheet. could you share that, emily?
[08:42] Emily: yes i'll grab a sample set, scrubbed of PII, and send to you by end of week.
[08:48] Aisha: great. for the pilot we can spin up a dedicated node in our trial environment, you'll get console access and the cost model sheet.
[08:57] Ravi: what's the expected time to provision the trial node?
[09:00] Marcus (SE): test nodes can be provisioned in ~48 hours once we have the basics and a short SOC checklist completed. for private/vpc it takes longer due to networking.
[09:11] Marcus Gomez: networking - we need SAML + SSO and rbac mapped to our idp.
[09:16] Aisha: we support SAML/Sso and can map RBAC roles, we'll send the integration guide.
[09:22] [09:22] Marcus (SE): last part of demo - show console cost breakdown: tokens by route, cost per route, and the optimize suggestions panel with recommended batching windows and cache sizing. (screen) here's an example suggestion: set batch window to 8-12ms for auth-route, allocate kv cache of 1.2GB for top prefixes, enable hash-redaction.
[09:43] Emily: curious about failure modes - if the cache node fails, is there a single point of failure?
[09:48] Marcus (SE): our runtime replicates cache entries across nodes and supports graceful degradation to compute-only mode. that said, for mission-critical you can enable multi-zone replicas.
[09:58] Ravi: ok this is all helpful. quick question on legal - is there a standard DPA we can get?
[10:03] Aisha: yes we'll include DPA and security pack in follow-up.
[10:07] [10:07] Marcus (SE): wrapping up, bottom line: for your traffic pattern - short seqs and high reuse - kv cache + small batching window on dedicated will likely give you the best latency and cost profile. pilot to validate hit rates and then scale.
[10:21] Emily: sounds good. can you include an example of the cost sensitivity if hit rate is only 30%?
[10:26] Marcus (SE): yes - we'll include that scenario in the spreadsheet; at 30% the win is smaller but still positive with batching.
[10:33] Ravi: thanks everyone. next steps?
[10:36] Aisha: recap - we'll send cost model spreadsheet, SOC2/KMS doc, and propose pilot dates. Marcus will provision a trial node. Emily will send prompt sample. we'll aim to have cost model and docs out by 2027-03-25.
[10:49] Marcus Gomez: thanks all.
[10:51] Aisha: thanks everyone - talk soon.
